titulo.en: He is boring, he is bored

objetivo.en: Describe a person's character and mood by distinguishing ser and estar with adjectives that change meaning.

traduccion.en: the personality

nota.en: Say “pehr-soh-nah-lee-DAHD”: stress the last syllable. The ending -dad matches English “-ty”: la personalidad, la realidad.

traduccion.en: the fan (of a team)

nota.en: Say “EEN-chah”: the h is silent. El hincha is for a man and la hincha for a woman. In Latin America hinchas are the fans of a soccer team.

traduccion.en: the goalkeeper

nota.en: For a woman: la portera. In much of Latin America, including Ecuador, people also say el arquero.

traduccion.en: the halftime

nota.en: Say “ehn-treh-TYEHM-poh”. A soccer match has two tiempos, and the break between them is el entretiempo.

traduccion.en: reserved, shy

nota.en: About a person, reservado means quiet and private. The same word also means “booked” for a table or a room, but not here.

traduccion.en: patient

nota.en: One form for men and women: un hombre paciente, una mujer paciente. Say “pah-SYEHN-teh”: the c sounds like s.

traduccion.en: calm, serene

nota.en: It is close to tranquilo but a little stronger: a sereno person stays calm even under pressure.

traduccion.en: brave

nota.en: One form for men and women. Say “bah-LYEHN-teh”: in Spanish v and b sound the same.

traduccion.en: fun, funny

nota.en: It changes with gender: divertido, divertida. It does not mean “diverted”: una persona divertida is fun to be with.

traduccion.en: boring (with ser); bored (with estar)

nota.en: Say “ah-boo-RREE-doh”. English uses two words, boring and bored; Spanish uses one word and lets ser or estar decide.

traduccion.en: clever (with ser); ready (with estar)

nota.en: It changes with gender: listo, lista. Es listo is about intelligence; está listo is about being ready.

explicacion.en: English has two different words, “bored” and “boring”, so learners keep ser for both. To say that someone is bored right now, use estar: está aburrido. Es aburrido means that the person is boring.
“Ready” is a state, not a quality, so it takes estar: la cena está lista. With ser, listo means “clever”.
Seguro with ser means “safe”, a quality of a place or thing: el barrio es seguro. With estar it means “sure”, a person’s certainty: estoy seguro.
English adjectives never change, so learners often add -o or -a to every adjective. Adjectives that end in -e, like paciente and valiente, have the same form for men and women.

titulo.en: Character with ser, mood with estar

texto.en: You already know that ser tells who or what someone is, and estar tells how someone is or where. With adjectives the same split applies: ser + adjective gives a lasting quality or character (Mateo es tranquilo y paciente), and estar + adjective gives a state or mood that can change (Mateo está cansado hoy). Most adjectives keep the same meaning with either verb. But a few adjectives change meaning with ser and estar: es aburrido means “he is boring”, and está aburrido means “he is bored”. English uses two different words (boring, bored; clever, ready), while Spanish has one adjective and the verb tells you which meaning you want.

titulo.en: More pairs that change meaning

texto.en: Four more pairs to learn: es listo (he is clever) and está listo (he is ready); es malo (he is bad, of character) and está malo (he is sick; this is the informal, colloquial way, and enfermo is the standard word; for food, está malo means it has gone bad); es rico (he is rich) and está rico (it tastes good); es seguro (it is safe) and está seguro (he is sure). Adjectives still agree: listo, lista; aburrido, aburrida. Adjectives that end in -e, such as paciente and valiente, have one form for men and women. Describe character with ser: tímido, paciente, tranquilo, valiente, divertido, reservado, sereno.

titulo.en: ser or estar: the meaning changes

texto.en: Same adjective, different meaning.

apoyo.en: sick (informal; enfermo is the standard word); spoiled (food)

contexto.en: Sunday afternoon in the living room of the Andrade family. Don Jorge, Emma and Mateo watch his team's match on TV. Emma and Mateo use usted with don Jorge; he uses tú with them, and Emma and Mateo use tú with each other.

dialogo.texto: Emma, Mateo, ya juega mi equipo. ¡Vamos a ver el partido!

traduccion.en: Emma, Mateo, my team is playing now. Let's watch the match!

dialogo.texto: ¡Qué bien, don Jorge! ¿Quién es el portero?

traduccion.en: How nice, don Jorge! Who is the goalkeeper?

dialogo.texto: Es ese chico alto. Es muy listo y muy valiente. Mi equipo va a ganar hoy.

traduccion.en: He is that tall guy. He is very clever and very brave. My team is going to win today.

dialogo.texto: Sí, don Jorge. Y los hinchas están muy contentos.

traduccion.en: Yes, don Jorge. And the fans are very happy.

dialogo.texto: Claro. Ya es el entretiempo. ¿Quieren un jugo?

traduccion.en: Of course. It is already halftime. Would you like a juice?

dialogo.texto: Sí, gracias, don Jorge. Mateo, ¿estás aburrido? Hoy estás muy callado.

traduccion.en: Yes, thank you, don Jorge. Mateo, are you bored? You are very quiet today.

dialogo.texto: No, Emma. No soy una persona aburrida. Es que hoy estoy cansado.

traduccion.en: No, Emma. I am not a boring person. It is just that I am tired today.

dialogo.texto: ¿Solo cansado? ¿No estás enfermo? ¿Estás malo?

traduccion.en: Just tired? You aren't sick? Are you ill?

dialogo.texto: No, estoy bien. Tengo mucho trabajo esta semana.

traduccion.en: No, I am fine. I have a lot of work this week.

dialogo.texto: Mateo, tú tienes una personalidad muy tranquila. Eres reservado, pero también eres divertido.

traduccion.en: Mateo, you have a very calm personality. You are reserved, but you are also fun.

dialogo.texto: Es verdad. Y don Jorge, el portero es sereno y valiente, ¿verdad?

traduccion.en: It's true. And don Jorge, the goalkeeper is calm and brave, isn't he?

dialogo.texto: Sí, nunca está nervioso. Mi hija Daniela es paciente, pero yo no soy paciente cuando juega mi equipo.

traduccion.en: Yes, he is never nervous. My daughter Daniela is patient, but I am not patient when my team plays.

dialogo.texto: Don Jorge, usted está muy contento hoy.

traduccion.en: Don Jorge, you are very happy today.

dialogo.texto: Claro. Y la señora Rosa dice que la cena está lista. Después del partido comemos todos juntos.

traduccion.en: Of course. And señora Rosa says that dinner is ready. After the match we all eat together.

dialogo.texto: ¡Qué bien! Estoy segura: hoy la cena va a estar muy rica.

traduccion.en: How nice! I'm sure: dinner is going to be very tasty today.

consigna.en: What does don Jorge say about the goalkeeper?

feedback.en: Don Jorge says: Es muy listo y muy valiente. With ser, listo is about intelligence, a quality of the goalkeeper.

consigna.en: Why is Mateo quiet?

feedback.en: Mateo says: Es que hoy estoy cansado. His mood today is a state, so he uses estar.

consigna.en: Choose the sentence that means “The goalkeeper is a clever person”.

feedback.en: A quality of the person takes ser: el portero es listo. El portero está listo means that he is ready.

consigna.en: Complete: “Mateo is not boring; he is just bored today.”

feedback.en: The first verb, es, is the quality; the missing one is a mood today, so: está.

titulo.en: The good thing and the best thing about the gym

objetivo.en: Evaluate a place or an activity with “lo” + adjective (lo bueno, lo malo, lo mejor de…).

traduccion.en: the membership

nota.en: Say “mehm-breh-SEE-ah”. In Ecuador you will also hear la suscripción for a monthly plan.

traduccion.en: the opening, the opening hour

nota.en: Say “ah-pehr-TOO-rah”. La hora de apertura is the time when a place opens.

traduccion.en: the monthly rate

nota.en: Mensual means “monthly”. La tarifa is the rate, the price list of a service.

traduccion.en: the trainer, the instructor (at a gym)

nota.en: For a woman: la monitora. In Ecuador entrenador is just as common. Careful: el monitor can also be a computer screen.

traduccion.en: the machine

nota.en: Say “MAH-kee-nah”: the stress is on the first syllable and the q is spelled with -u-.

traduccion.en: the weight-training routine

nota.en: Las pesas are the weights. La rutina is a set plan of exercises, not only a daily routine.

traduccion.en: the dumbbell

nota.en: Say “mahn-KWEHR-nah”. It is the usual word in Mexico and Ecuador for a hand weight.

traduccion.en: the loud music

nota.en: Literally “high music”: alto means both “tall” and “loud” when you talk about sound.

traduccion.en: the monthly fee

nota.en: Say “mehn-swah-lee-DAHD”. It is what you pay each month for a membership.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Lo buena es la música alta.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Lo bueno es la música alta.

explicacion.en: English speakers want to make the adjective agree with the noun that follows (música is feminine). But lo always goes with the masculine singular form: lo bueno, lo malo, lo mejor, whatever the noun is.
English says “the good thing” with a noun, so learners use la or el. Spanish uses lo + adjective to talk about an idea or a quality without naming a noun: lo bueno.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Lo mejor sobre el gimnasio es el horario.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Lo mejor del gimnasio es el horario.

explicacion.en: English says “the best thing about the gym”, and learners translate about with sobre. Spanish uses de: lo mejor de + noun, and de + el becomes del.

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Lo bueno es que abre temprano.

explicacion.en: English often leaves out “that”, but Spanish keeps que when a full clause follows: lo bueno es que abre temprano.
English says “the hard part is starting”, with -ing. After lo + adjective + es, Spanish uses the infinitive: lo difícil es empezar.

titulo.en: lo + adjective: the good thing, the bad thing

texto.en: To talk about a quality or an idea without naming a noun, Spanish puts lo before a masculine singular adjective: lo bueno (the good thing, the good part), lo malo (the bad thing), lo difícil (the hard part). It never changes, even when the noun you mention next is feminine: lo bueno es la música. To rate a place you also have lo mejor and lo peor, which you already know as “better” and “worse”, now with lo: the best thing, the worst thing. After de, de + el becomes del: lo mejor del gimnasio.

titulo.en: What comes after lo + adjective + es

texto.en: After lo bueno es… you can put three things. A noun: Lo bueno es el horario. The word que and a full sentence: Lo bueno es que abre temprano. Or an infinitive: Lo difícil es empezar. Do not use -ing as in English (“the hard part is starting”): after es, Spanish uses the infinitive, empezar. For something very strong, remember -ísimo from earlier: este gimnasio es carísimo means “very, very expensive”. Do not add muy before it.

titulo.en: Review: better, worse and very, very

texto.en: You already know these forms. Now you will use them with lo.

apoyo.en: better; with lo: the best thing
worse; with lo: the worst thing

dialogo.texto: Con mucho gusto. La apertura es a las cinco de la mañana y cerramos a las diez de la noche. La tarifa mensual es de cuarenta dólares.

titulo.en: I learned by playing

objetivo.en: Explain how something is done or was learned using a manner gerund, and congratulate someone on their effort.

traduccion.en: the midfielder

nota.en: In Latin America el volante is a midfield player. It is also the steering wheel of a car, so context tells you which one.

traduccion.en: the goal (the frame)

nota.en: In Ecuador the goal frame is el arco, and the goalkeeper is the person who guards it. Do not mix it up with el gol.

traduccion.en: the stands

nota.en: Say “tree-BOO-nah”. It is the part of the stadium where the fans sit.

traduccion.en: the fans (as a group)

nota.en: Say “een-CHAH-dah”: the h is silent. La hinchada is all the fans together; one fan is el hincha.

traduccion.en: the league

nota.en: Say “LEE-gah”: the g before a sounds hard, as in “go”.

traduccion.en: the goal (the score)

nota.en: Say “gohl”. Meter un gol is to score a goal.

traduccion.en: the linesman, the assistant referee

nota.en: Say “hwehs deh LEE-neh-ah”: j sounds like a strong h. For a woman: la jueza de línea.

traduccion.en: the play, the move

nota.en: A jugada is one action in the game. It comes from jugar.

traduccion.en: the free kick

nota.en: Tiro means “shot”, and libre means “free”. Say “TEE-roh LEE-breh”.

traduccion.en: the penalty kick

nota.en: Say “peh-NAHL”: stress the last syllable. In Spain you will also hear el penalti.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Aprendí español por hablar con Daniela.

explicacion.en: English says “by talking” and learners translate by with por. To say how you did something, Spanish uses the gerund alone: hablando, mirando, entrenando.
English can use -ing as a noun (“Running is hard”). In Spanish the gerund tells how an action happens; as a subject you use the infinitive: correr es difícil.
A gerund cannot end in -iendo after a vowel: the i becomes y. So leer gives leyendo, and creer gives creyendo.
Some -ir verbs change the stem in the gerund: dormir gives durmiendo, pedir gives pidiendo, decir gives diciendo. Learners usually keep the stem of the infinitive.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Llevo un mes trabajar en Andes Vivos.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Llevo un mes trabajando en Andes Vivos.

explicacion.en: After llevar + time you need the gerund, not the infinitive: llevo un mes trabajando means “I have been working for a month”.

titulo.en: The gerund tells how

texto.en: To say how you do or did something, Spanish uses a verb ending in -ando or -iendo: Aprendí a jugar mirando a mi papá (by watching my dad). English uses by + -ing; Spanish uses the gerund alone, with no por and no preposition. To make it, take off -ar and add -ando (jugar, jugando); take off -er or -ir and add -iendo (correr, corriendo; escribir, escribiendo). The question is ¿Cómo?, and the answer is the gerund: ¿Cómo aprendiste? Hablando con Daniela.

titulo.en: Irregular gerunds and a warning

texto.en: Four common gerunds are irregular: leer gives leyendo, dormir gives durmiendo, decir gives diciendo and pedir gives pidiendo. Do not confuse this use with estar + gerund, which you already know for an action in progress: Estoy corriendo ahora (I am running now). With a manner gerund the action is usually in the past or the present, but the gerund answers “how”: Mejoré entrenando todos los días. With llevar + time, the gerund says how long: Llevo un mes trabajando. The gerund is never used as a noun: for “Running is hard”, say Correr es difícil.

titulo.en: Making the gerund

texto.en: Take the infinitive and change its ending.

titulo.en: Let's go to the beach!

objetivo.en: Suggest a leisure plan to a group with the “let's” imperative (¡vamos!, salgamos, hagámoslo).

traduccion.en: the beach town, the seaside resort

nota.en: Say “bahl-neh-AH-ryoh”. In Ecuador and much of Latin America it is a place by the sea or a river where people go to swim.

traduccion.en: the sunscreen

nota.en: Solar means “of the sun”. Protector is the thing that protects you: el protector solar.

traduccion.en: the beach umbrella

nota.en: Sombra is shade, and a sombrilla gives you shade. Say “sohm-BREE-yah”: ll sounds like the y in “yes”.

traduccion.en: the towel

nota.en: Say “toh-AH-yah”: ll sounds like the y in “yes”.

traduccion.en: the sandals

nota.en: Spanish uses the plural here, as in English: las sandalias, unas sandalias.

traduccion.en: the sand

nota.en: Say “ah-REH-nah”. In Spanish la arena is always singular.

traduccion.en: the wave

nota.en: Say “OH-lah”. Do not mix it up with hola: the h is silent, and ola has no h.

traduccion.en: to swim in the sea, to go for a swim

nota.en: The ñ sounds like “ny” in “canyon”. Bañarse is a reflexive verb: me baño, te bañas, se baña.

traduccion.en: to sunbathe

nota.en: Literally “to take the sun”. Say “toh-MAR ehl sohl”.

traduccion.en: the very early start

nota.en: Say “mah-droo-GOHN”. It comes from madrugar, to get up very early. ¡Qué madrugón! means “What an early start!”

explicacion.en: The nosotros command takes the subjunctive, and with -ir and -er verbs the ending is -amos: salgamos, comamos, hagamos. Only -ar verbs use -emos: compremos, nademos, esperemos. Learners often mix up the two endings.
Compramos means “we buy”. To say “let’s buy”, use the subjunctive form: compremos.
In an affirmative command, the pronoun is attached to the verb: hagamos + lo = hagámoslo. The stress stays on ga, so you need the written accent. Do not write the pronoun as a separate word.
In a negative command, the pronoun goes before the verb as a separate word, with no accent: no lo dejemos. The attached form is only for affirmative commands.
English says “Let’s swim” with no extra word, so learners drop the a. Vamos + a + infinitive is the fixed structure.

titulo.en: Let's…: vamos and the nosotros command

texto.en: To suggest a plan to a group you can say Vamos a + place or infinitive: ¡Vamos a la playa! ¡Vamos a nadar! This is the everyday way to say “let’s go” and “let’s…”. For other verbs Spanish has the nosotros command, which looks like the nosotros form of the subjunctive: salgamos (let’s leave), compremos (let’s buy), comamos (let’s eat), hagamos (let’s do). Notice the endings: -ar verbs change to -emos (comprar, compremos; nadar, nademos), while -er and -ir verbs change to -amos (comer, comamos; salir, salgamos). For ir, the everyday affirmative command is vamos (vayamos exists, but it sounds formal and is rare).

titulo.en: Pronouns, accents and the negative

texto.en: With a pronoun, the affirmative command attaches it to the end of the verb, and the stress does not move, so the word gets a written accent: hagamos + lo = hagámoslo (let’s do it); compremos + lo = comprémoslo. In the negative the pronoun stays in front of the verb as a separate word, and there is no accent: No esperemos más (let’s not wait any longer); No lo dejemos para después (let’s not leave it for later). To accept an invitation you already know Sí, con mucho gusto; to turn it down, No, lo siento or Tal vez otro día.

titulo.en: Some, none, any

objetivo.en: Ask and answer about vague quantities of people or things using alguno, ninguno and cualquier(a) on a beach day.

traduccion.en: some, any, one of them (pronoun)

nota.en: Alguno is masculine and alguna feminine: ¿Alguno de ustedes…? / ¿Alguna de ustedes…? Alguno is also the full form that is shortened to algún before a noun.

traduccion.en: none, not one (pronoun)

nota.en: Ninguno, ninguna. Say “neen-GOO-noh”. It is almost always singular: ninguno de nosotros.

traduccion.en: some place, any place

nota.en: Alguno loses its -o before a masculine singular noun: algún lugar. With a feminine noun it does not change: alguna playa.

traduccion.en: no problem, not any problem

nota.en: Same shortening as algún: ningún problema. Feminine: ninguna toalla.

traduccion.en: any day

nota.en: Cualquier goes before a noun, masculine or feminine: cualquier día, cualquier hora. It has no -a and no plural form in this use.

traduccion.en: any one, whichever

nota.en: Cualquiera alone means “any one of them”: Cualquiera sirve. Say “kwahl-KYEH-rah”.

traduccion.en: the kiosk, the small stand

nota.en: Say “KYOHS-koh”. A kiosco is a small stand that sells drinks, snacks and sunscreen on the beach.

traduccion.en: the beach bag

nota.en: La bolsa is a bag. In Ecuador a bolsa is also a plastic bag from the store.

traduccion.en: the snack

nota.en: Say “reh-free-heh-RYOH”: the g sounds like a strong h. In Ecuador a refrigerio is a light meal between two meals.

explicacion.en: Algún only appears directly before a masculine singular noun: algún lugar. When alguno stands alone as a pronoun, it keeps its -o: alguno de ustedes.

English does not allow a double negative (“I don’t have none”), but Spanish needs no before the verb when ninguno comes after it: no tengo ninguno. If ninguno comes first, there is no no: Ninguno tiene.
Before a masculine singular noun, alguno becomes algún, and ninguno becomes ningún: algún restaurante, ningún problema.
Before a noun the form is cualquier, without -a: cualquier día, cualquier hora. Cualquiera is used alone: cualquiera sirve.
Ninguno is shortened to ningún before a masculine singular noun. The double negative no hay ningún is normal in Spanish.

titulo.en: Alguno, ninguno: one of a group

texto.en: Use alguno/alguna to ask if one person or thing in a group does something, and ninguno/ninguna to say that none does. You usually add de + the group: ¿Alguno de ustedes tiene protector solar? — Ninguno. Before a masculine singular noun, alguno and ninguno lose their -o: algún lugar, ningún problema. Feminine nouns do not change: alguna playa, ninguna toalla. With ninguno after the verb Spanish needs the double negative: No tengo ninguno. If ninguno comes before the verb there is only one negative: Ninguno tiene.

titulo.en: Cualquier and cualquiera: any at all

texto.en: Cualquier means “any (at all)” and goes before a noun, masculine or feminine: cualquier día, cualquier hora, cualquier tienda. Alone, it is cualquiera and means “any one of them”: Cualquiera sirve. Do not confuse cualquier with algún. Algún lugar is “some place”; cualquier lugar is “any place you like”. In this class you also recycle the double negative, the pronouns lo, la, los, las (No lo traje) and the let’s-command: compremos.
